transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Luca Rossi (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Cascade - Platform Eng), Daniel Foster (Cascade - Head of ML), Aisha Romero (Cascade - SecOps), Tom Nguyen (Cascade - Dev Advocate)
---
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, we really appreciate you taking the time. I'm Maya Chen, AE at Redwood, and with me is Luca Rossi, our solutions engineer. Quick check audio/video ok?
[00:12] Priya: Yep can hear you, loud and clear.
[00:15] Daniel: All good here.
[00:18] Maya: Great. The goal for today is to understand your integration constraints — SDKs, how you plan to use LangChain or LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy setup, rate-limits, and observability needs — and then surface what a pilot could look like.
[00:31] Priya: Perfect. To kick off, our current stack: we run a Node/Go backend, we have an Envoy edge proxy that handles auth and rate-limiting today, and ML infra is on-prem with some GCP for batch jobs. We're evaluating Redwood to replace our current hosted LLM endpoints because cost and latency are starting to balloon.
[00:50] Luca: Got it — thanks. Quick clarifying question: when you say "hosted LLM endpoints" is that OpenAI or a mix?
[00:57] Priya: Mostly OpenAI for now, some Phi- hosted smaller models for internal tasks. We've also trialed Anthropic for assistant-type flows.
[01:06] Daniel: The big thing for us is telemetry and predictable cost per inference. We need token-level breakdowns to tie to product feature flags.
[01:15] Maya: That's exactly one of Redwood's focus areas — token-level cost and latency breakdowns are surfaced in Console, and we can also export traces to your Datadog. We'll share a sample dashboard.
[01:28] Tom: A few constraints: we have a security requirement for key management — KMS-backed keys — and our SecOps wants an option for private deployment inside our VPC or Dedicated hardware if needed. Can you speak to Redwood Private vs Dedicated?
[01:43] Luca: Sure. High level: Hosted is our managed cloud offering, fastest to get started. Dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools (predictable throughput and isolation), and Private is a VPC/on-prem package where the control plane is private. For KMS, we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for Private and have BYOK options for Dedicated as well. There may be slight differences in audit log retention depending on package.
[02:06] Aisha: When you say "integrate with KMS" are we talking envelope encryption or full disk? We need to know scope for compliance.
[02:12] Luca: We typically support envelope encryption for model artifacts and customer key wrapping for request-level secrets. For full disk encryption on on-prem, that's on your infra side but Redwood's runtime can be configured to use keys via the HSM/KMS. I'll follow up with the exact cryptographic model in writing.
[02:28] Priya: Great. On integration, we've standardized on LangChain for our orchestration in Python, and for search we use LlamaIndex-derived flows. Can Redwood fit into that ecosystem easily?
[02:39] Luca: Yes, we have SDKs for Python, Node, and Go. We also provide LangChain + LlamaIndex adapters — I can share examples. For most customers we provide a small drop-in wrapper so the chain can call the Redwood SDK as if it were any other provider. There are some gotchas around streaming and function calling that we document.
[02:58] Daniel: Streaming is important for UX. We do partial display of tokens as they arrive. How does Redwood handle streaming with latency targets and batching?
[03:08] Luca: Good question — our runtime supports streaming at the token level while still doing continuous batching under the hood. You configure SLOs: if you want <100ms first-byte we can route to lower-batch paths, otherwise batching will coalesce requests to improve throughput. There's a balance — lower latency generally increases per-token cost.
[03:27] Tom: On the gateway side, can we keep our Envoy edge and put Redwood behind it? We want to do rate-limits and per-customer quotas at the proxy level.
[03:35] Maya: Yes you can put Redwood behind Envoy or use Redwood as the upstream. Many customers keep their proxy for auth/routing and call Redwood's API over TLS. We also have an on-prem sidecar option for Private deployments to keep traffic internal.
[03:48] Priya: Any guidance for how to handle KV cache warming? We have a lot of short context prompts where prefix caching would help.
[03:55] Luca: Redwood supports KV cache management; the runtime can persist and reuse prefix caches if you pin model versions. For short prompts, we recommend prefix caching plus client-side heuristics to reuse session tokens. We'll share a doc with cache TTLs and example heuristics.
[04:10] Daniel: Our perf team also wants to run a realistic benchmark — 1k concurrent sessions, average prompt 120 tokens, 30 token responses — and compare Hosted vs Dedicated latency and cost. Can Redwood support that?
[04:21] Luca: Absolutely. We can provision a pilot environment and coordinate a benchmark. For Dedicated we can mirror production GPU instance types to give apples-to-apples comparisons. We'll need your traffic profile and a few representative prompts.
[04:33] Priya: Good. On rate limits: we prefer token-based quota rather than request-count. Can we do both? We have some legacy systems that only count requests.
[04:42] Maya: Console supports both. You can set token quotas per-API-key or route, and we expose usage APIs so you can enforce request-based logic upstream if you need to.
[04:51] Aisha: Observability — we need trace correlation. How do we propagate trace IDs and get token-level timing?
[04:58] Luca: We accept traceparent headers and will surface per-request spans. Token-level timing is available in the trace payloads; sample size is configurable to control payload volume. We export to OpenTelemetry -> Datadog/Jaeger.
[05:10] Tom: How about schema for function calling and structured outputs? We use function calling heavily for agent orchestration.
[05:17] Luca: Supported. We have built-in function/tool-calling capability and structured output hints. There are a few versioning differences across open models; our SDK normalizes those and returns a consistent payload. Streaming function call events are supported.
[05:30] Priya: Are there any mis-compatibilities with LlamaIndex when using chunked embeddings or rerankers? We've had some mismatch in tokenization and id mapping previously.
[05:41] Luca: Tokenization differences can happen if you mix model families. We recommend standardizing on the same tokenizer or using Redwood's embedding pipeline which normalizes token boundaries. For reranking, we provide a rerank endpoint that integrates with LlamaIndex callbacks. I'll add a note in the sample repo about consistent tokenizers.
[05:57] Daniel: Security question — SSO: can we use SAML/Okta for console access and RBAC?
[06:03] Maya: Yes, SAML/Okta is supported for Console SSO and we have RBAC roles (admin, dev, viewer). For API keys we can map teams and apply per-team quotas.
[06:12] Aisha: Do you have an SOC2 report we can share with procurement?
[06:16] Maya: We do. I'll attach the SOC 2 summary and a security pack.
[06:21] Priya: Billing model — how does token counting work across streaming responses? There are weird cases when partial tokens are sent.
[06:28] Luca: We bill per generated token and per input token; streaming doesn't change the accounting model — we charge for what the model actually generates. Small differences can occur across codecs but it's normalized in Console.
[06:39] Tom: Ok on SDK specifics: we use a mono-repo in Node and Python. Are there multi-tenant client libs or best practices for client key rotation?
[06:48] Luca: We have examples for key rotation and multi-tenant patterns. For high-scale multi-tenant you typically put Redwood behind your tenant gateway and mint short-lived per-tenant keys that your gateway uses. That lets you keep tenant isolation and do per-tenant quotas.
[07:03] Priya: On the Dedicated side — can we bring our own models? We have a fine-tuned model family locked behind license.
[07:10] Luca: BYOM is supported in Dedicated and Private, with a model onboarding process. There are licensing considerations and we need to validate the model format. For highly-custom models you may need an on-prem path. We'll list the supported formats in the follow-up.
[07:22] Daniel: What about quantization and token quality tradeoffs? We sometimes need int8 for cost but worry about hallucination increase.
[07:30] Luca: We provide quantization profiles and run per-workload evals. Redwood Optimize can recommend profiles based on your prompt sets. We surface quality regressions tied to eval prompts so you can see the impact.
[07:43] Maya: Quick interjection — I want to make sure we capture success criteria. Priya, can you outline what would make a pilot successful for Cascade?
[07:49] Priya: Sure: 1) replace current endpoint without regression in latency for the top 10 customer flows, 2) tokenized cost reduction of at least 20% for batch workloads, 3) clear audit logs and key management flow documented for our security team, and 4) integration with LangChain/LlamaIndex with minimal code changes.
[08:08] Maya: Great, that's very actionable. We'll map the pilot to those success criteria.
[08:15] Tom: One more nit: rate-limit backpressure behavior. If a tenant hits quota, do we return 429s or queue? We prefer graceful degradation rather than lots of 429s.
[08:24] Luca: You can configure backpressure policies — immediate 429, token-leaky bucket, or queueing with SLA-based eviction. For user-facing latency-sensitive endpoints we usually recommend soft quotas plus an adaptive fallback to a smaller model.
[08:38] Priya: Fallbacks sound useful. Would you be able to demonstrate a canary rollout with fallback during the pilot?
[08:44] Luca: Yes, rollouts are supported — canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to a cheaper model when latency or errors spike. We'll include a rollout plan in the pilot doc.
[08:56] Daniel: Regarding observability hooks again — can we get token-level cost exported to our billing system?
[09:02] Maya: You can push usage webhooks or pull via an API; token-level breakdown is exportable as CSV or JSON. We'll include a sample webhook payload.
[09:11] Aisha: For Private deployment latency, does Redwood require a control plane VS data plane split? We're sensitive about egress.
[09:19] Luca: For Private we typically run a local data plane in your VPC and keep an optional control plane. If you require fully air-gapped, we offer an on-prem package where both control and data planes are customer-hosted.
[09:31] Tom: Any caveats on model updates? If we pin a model and then want a security patch in the runtime, how is that handled?
[09:38] Luca: Rollouts can be decoupled — you can pin model versions independently from runtime updates. Security patches to the runtime are pushed but we maintain compatibility and provide change logs; Dedicated and Private have patch windows coordinated with the customer.
[09:51] Priya: Ok this is super helpful. Can we dig briefly into the LangChain adapter? For example, how we wire up the chain to use Redwood's streaming callbacks?
[09:58] Luca: Sure — at a high level you pass the Redwood client into the LLM wrapper, enable streaming callbacks in the chain, and implement the on_new_token callback to write partial outputs. One nuance: for function-calling flows you may need to buffer until invocation completes if you want structured arguments. I'll send a code snippet.
[10:17] Priya: Lovely. Any gotchas with token accounting when using streaming + function calls? We had double-counting issues before.
[10:25] Luca: Double-counting is usually a client-side bookkeeping bug — our SDK exposes accurate token usage after the call and the streaming events include incremental token deltas. We'll show an example of correct accounting.
[10:37] Maya: Quick recap — items we will deliver: SOC 2 summary & security pack, Dedicated vs Hosted pricing matrix, LangChain/LlamaIndex adapter samples + GH link, pilot benchmarking plan and rollouts doc, and sample webhook for usage exports. Anything else?
[10:54] Priya: Please include the VPC topology diagram and KMS integration details.
[10:58] Aisha: And encryption details for how keys are used in runtime.
[11:02] Maya: Noted. We'll get that to you.
[11:05] Tom: Timeline question — if we sign for a pilot, how quickly can you stand up a Dedicated sandbox?
[11:10] Luca: For Dedicated pilot we can typically stand up reserved capacity in 7-10 business days once contracts and payment are done. Hosted sandbox can be immediate. Private on-prem takes longer depending on procurement.
[11:21] Daniel: Ok, procurement and legal will want SLA language and an exit data deletion process.
[11:26] Maya: We'll include the retention and data deletion procedures in the security pack.
[11:30] Priya: One small operational ask: do you expose a self-serve key rotation API? Right now our platform rotates keys nightly.
[11:37] Luca: Yes, we have an API for creating, rotating, and revoking keys. We'll share the endpoint docs and an example script.
[11:45] Aisha: We might run an internal security review first; if anything else comes up we'll send questions to you.
[11:50] Maya: Sounds good. Final quick check — any blockers that would prevent you from running a pilot?
[11:55] Priya: I think our main blocker is procurement lead time. Also we need KMS specifics to sign off. But tech-wise we're good.
[12:04] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the artifacts and propose pilot dates. Thanks everyone for the time.
[12:11] Daniel: Thanks folks, bye.
---
End of transcript.
Notes: occasional ASR errors (product names misheard), some speaker labels guessed. Follow-up attachments: SOC2_summary.pdf (link placeholder), langchain_adapter_sample.zip (link placeholder), dedicated_pricing_matrix.xlsx (link placeholder).
